questions.q: What does 'syllabic' word setting mean?
options: One note is sung to each syllable of text
Many notes are sung to one syllable
The words are spoken rather than sung
Each word is repeated three times
questions.explain: Syllabic setting gives one note per syllable, making the words easy to hear.

questions.q: What is 'melismatic' word setting?
options: Many notes sung to a single syllable
A syllable sung on a spoken pitch
questions.explain: A melisma stretches one syllable over several notes for decorative or expressive effect.

questions.q: Which term describes setting a syllable to a small group of about two to four notes?
questions.explain: Neumatic setting places a short group of notes on a syllable, between syllabic and melismatic.

questions.q: What is meant by 'text painting' (word painting)?
options: Music that reflects the literal meaning of the words being sung
Writing the lyrics in a decorative script
Setting every syllable to a single note
Repeating the chorus after each verse
questions.explain: Text painting makes the music mirror the meaning of the words, such as a falling line on 'descend'.

questions.q: A composer sets the word 'rising' to an ascending scale. This is an example of what?
questions.explain: An ascending line on 'rising' illustrates the word's meaning, which is word painting.

questions.q: A composer wants the words of a congregational hymn to be clearly understood. Which word setting is most suitable?
questions.explain: Syllabic setting (one note per syllable) keeps the words clear for the congregation.

questions.q: A composer wants to emphasise and decorate the important word 'glory' in a choral work. Which technique is most likely used?
questions.explain: Spreading 'glory' over many notes (a melisma) highlights and ornaments the key word.

questions.q: In opera and oratorio, what is an aria?
options: A solo song that expresses a character's emotions
A spoken passage with no singing
A dance for the full orchestra
questions.explain: An aria is an expressive solo song that reflects a character's feelings rather than advancing the plot.

questions.q: What is recitative?
options: A speech-like vocal style that advances the story
An elaborate solo showing off the voice
A section sung by the whole chorus
questions.explain: Recitative uses speech-like rhythms and simple accompaniment to carry the narrative forward.

questions.q: What is the overall structure of a da capo aria?
questions.explain: A da capo aria repeats the opening A section after a contrasting B section, giving an ABA form.

questions.q: In choral music, what do the letters SATB stand for?
questions.explain: SATB names the four standard choral voice parts from highest to lowest.

questions.q: What is the main difference between recitative and aria?
options: Recitative is speech-like and moves the plot, while an aria is lyrical and expresses emotion
Recitative is for chorus, while an aria is for orchestra
Recitative uses many notes per syllable, while an aria is syllabic
Recitative is always faster than an aria
questions.explain: Recitative narrates in a speech-like way, whereas the aria pauses the action to explore feeling.

questions.q: What is a chorale?
options: A hymn tune, usually sung in homophonic four-part harmony
A solo aria with elaborate ornamentation
questions.explain: A chorale is a hymn-like melody harmonised in blocks, associated with Lutheran church music.

questions.q: What does the term 'coloratura' describe?
options: Elaborate, rapid and highly ornamented vocal writing
Plain syllabic singing of a hymn
questions.explain: Coloratura features fast runs, trills and decoration that display a singer's agility.

questions.q: What is a 'Lied'?
options: A German art song for solo voice and piano
A large-scale choral work for church
A group dance in triple time
questions.explain: A Lied is a German song for one voice and piano, often setting a poem expressively.

questions.q: What is 'strophic' form in a song?
options: The same music is repeated for each verse of the text
New music is written for every line of text
Only the chorus is ever repeated
The voice speaks rather than sings
questions.explain: In strophic form each verse uses the same melody, even though the words change.

questions.q: What does 'through-composed' mean?
options: New music is used throughout, with no repetition of whole verses
Every verse is sung to the same tune
The song has no words at all
Only instruments play, with no voice
questions.explain: A through-composed song sets fresh music as the text unfolds, following its changing meaning.

questions.q: A folk ballad tells a long story across ten verses, each sung to exactly the same tune. Which form is this?
questions.explain: Repeating one tune for every verse of the story is strophic form.

questions.q: A composer wants the music to follow the shifting emotions of a dramatic poem, never repeating a whole section. Which form best suits this?
questions.explain: Through-composed form lets the music change continuously to match the poem's developing mood.

questions.q: In a typical pop song using verse-chorus form, how do the verse and chorus usually relate to the words?
options: The chorus repeats with the same words and music, while each verse has new words
The verse always repeats the same words, while the chorus changes each time
Both verse and chorus keep exactly the same words throughout
Neither the verse nor the chorus is ever repeated
questions.explain: The recurring chorus provides a memorable hook, while the verses advance the lyrics with new words.
